newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian army and bedouin vote on constitution.
newsitem.headline: Algerian army and bedouin vote on constitution.

text.p: Over 500,000 members of Algeria's security forces and bedouin in remote areas began voting on Monday on a draft constitution, Algerian radio said.

The early vote will free the military to protect voters against possible Moslem guerrillas when the national vote is held on Thursday. Guerrillas, who want to disrupt election day, have warned people to stay in their homes.
Caravans of cars carrying election officials left late on Sunday to travel through thousands of kilometres (miles) to reach bedouin in remote areas.

"They start Sunday because they have a long trip of 1,800 km (1,125 miles) to go to meet voters," said Embarak Essadi, an election official in the southwestern town of Tindouf as his men headed off in a seven-car caravan that made up the polling station.

Algerian expatriates in Europe and other Arab countries began voting on Sunday. Algerian state television showed voters lining up in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Brussels and Bonn. Voters said they were pained by the killing at home and hoped their vote would help restore peace.

Officials said television images in last year's presidential vote of expatriates flooding polling stations despite snow and heavy rain encouraged voters at home to turn up in defiance of Moslem guerrilla death threats.

Government officials and their backers stepped up a campaign for voters to endorse the constitutional changes. The draft, if approved by more than 50 percent of the 16.4 million electorate who vote, will broaden the president's paramount powers but limits him to two-five year terms.

It bans politicians from campaigning as representatives of Islam or the Arab or Berber communities. Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia said on Sunday during a campaign rally in Bouzerah in Algiers the draft constitution aims to strengthen a multiparty democracy in a united nation.
Assailed by complaints of corruption and bureaucracy, Ouyahia ordered an official probe of local authorities in Bouzerah.

Secular opposition firebrand Said Saadi, casting doubt on the election, told the Algerian Liberte newspaper on Monday that national authorities had urged Algiers' local officials to "ban the slighest (independent) presence in the offices where the ballots will be counted."
Although the government insists the poll will be held in "full freedom and tranquility," violence continued unabated in the days before the poll.

A car bomb killed five people and wounded 19 on Sunday in the central garrison town of Blida, newspapers said on Monday. Security forces killed nine guerrillas in two operations in the previous 24 hours near Algiers, newspapers also reported.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
